strengths: Originality/significance: Framing time-series question answering as iterative, question-conditioned segment acquisition is a useful direction. The shared controller–reasoner policy and reliability reward based on repeated reasoner rollouts are interesting contributions.

Soundness: The method is described with equations, an algorithm, role-specific rewards, and ablations. Results cover six benchmarks from several domains, and the reported average accuracy gain over the strongest baseline by average score is substantial.
Presentation: The motivation and controller–reasoner interaction are generally clear, and the qualitative examples make the intended behavior understandable.

The authors report important negative results, including ARTIST's large deficit to TimeMaster+RL on Sleep-QA, and acknowledge extra inference cost and restriction to univariate, regularly sampled series.
The appendix provides prompts, dataset sizes, LoRA settings, RL batch and rollout counts, temperatures, KL coefficient, training duration, and hardware, offering a partial basis for reproduction.
weaknesses: Soundness: The experiments do not isolate the central claim that adaptive selection itself causes the gains. There is no equal-budget comparison against random, uniform, fixed, learned one-shot, or oracle segment selection. The main “Reasoner Only” ablation processes the full series under a different input regime, so its 9.30-point deficit can reflect context length, training distribution, or architecture rather than adaptivity. The other ablations are reported on only two of six datasets, and segment quality is never evaluated against localization evidence.

The efficiency/selective-consumption claim is misleading. Equations (3)–(4) and the controller prompt explicitly give the controller the full time-series embedding at every interaction. Thus the system does consume and encode the full series, potentially repeatedly; Figure 3 measures only the fraction forwarded as selected segments. No latency, FLOPs, token count, memory, or end-to-end compute comparison supports an efficiency benefit.

Figure 3 does not establish that limited coverage improves accuracy. Its bins are observational and confounded by question difficulty: difficult questions may cause both broader retrieval and lower accuracy. The manuscript nevertheless interprets this correlation causally as evidence that concentrated selection improves performance.

Statistical evidence is inadequate. Although the paper claims eight independent runs, it reports neither standard deviations, confidence intervals, per-run results, nor significance tests. Most test sets contain only about 200 examples, making several small gains—such as 1.26 points on Sleep-QA—unconvincing. It is also unclear whether “runs” are independent training seeds or repeated stochastic inference.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The reward weights w_D, w_f, w_c, and w_e are not specified; nor are the pretraining data/configuration, number and filtering procedure of GPT-5-generated traces, maximum interaction rounds, segment-length constraints at RL/inference time, decoding/evaluation details, or baseline tuning procedures. The added ETI/1TS construction is underspecified, and no code or artifact is identified. Variance-guided sampling p(g) proportional to reward variance is undefined when every group's variance is zero.

There are technical and reporting inconsistencies. The policy objectives condition only on q and previous same-role output tokens, omitting the time series, selected segments, and cross-role history defined earlier. The Sleep-QA description states five merged classes, while the random-guess accuracy is 16.67%, corresponding to six balanced choices. TRQA accuracy is 83.06 in Table 1 but 83.34 in Table 2. F1 averaging is undefined, and some F1 values are difficult to reconcile with the corresponding accuracies.

Baseline fairness is insufficiently documented. Systems differ in backbone size, modality, access to summary statistics, and task-specific fine-tuning, but training budgets and input truncation are not controlled. The claimed 6.46-point improvement is the difference between ARTIST and the single baseline with the best overall average, not the average gain over the strongest comparator on each dataset; the wording and Table 1 footnote suggest the latter.

Presentation is readable at a high level, but crucial operational details are deferred or absent, while Figure 2 is visually dense. Calling the setup “self-play” is also debatable because both roles optimize against supervised ground-truth correctness rather than creating tasks or an evolving opponent.

Limitations and ethics are treated too narrowly. The generic impact statement says no consequences need highlighting despite evaluation on ECG and EEG tasks. Clinical misuse, calibration, subgroup robustness, dataset bias, and the reliability implications of selecting only partial physiological signals deserve discussion. The limitations also omit the controller's full-series access and the lack of demonstrated computational savings.

Overall, the idea is promising and the headline results merit further study, but unsupported causal and efficiency claims, missing controls, statistical uncertainty, and substantial reproducibility gaps prevent reliable acceptance in its current form.

strengths: Originality: The controller–reasoner formulation is a plausible and relatively novel adaptation of active information acquisition and hierarchical reinforcement learning to time-series question answering. Separating where to inspect from how to answer is well motivated.

Significance: Adaptive temporal localization could be useful for long signals, and the evaluation spans six datasets from several domains. ARTIST obtains strong aggregate accuracy, with especially large gains on TSQA, and the ablations suggest that reliability rewards and trajectory-level optimization matter.

Presentation: The main architecture, interaction protocol, rewards, and two-stage training pipeline are generally explained clearly. The paper provides prompts, dataset statistics, qualitative examples, and several component ablations.

The manuscript candidly identifies extra inference cost and the restriction to univariate, regularly sampled signals; these are appropriate limitations and should not themselves count against the work.
weaknesses: Soundness: The central selective-data-use interpretation is not supported by the actual architecture. The controller receives the full time-series embedding at every round and can request the entire sequence, as it does in a Figure 4 example. ARTIST therefore imposes a communication bottleneck between controller and reasoner rather than actively avoiding access to or processing of the full signal. Claims about consuming only 30–70% of the input and improving efficiency are misleading without end-to-end compute, latency, token, and memory measurements.

Soundness: Figure 3 is observational: difficult questions may cause both greater coverage and lower accuracy. Its accuracy-versus-coverage correlation cannot establish the claimed causal conclusion that concentrating on fewer segments improves performance. There is also no reward for selection cost, no oracle segment-relevance evaluation, and no shuffled, irrelevant, or masked-segment control demonstrating that answers are grounded in the retrieved segments rather than question priors or information already encoded by the controller.

Soundness: The key comparison does not isolate adaptive selection. ARTIST uses GPT-5-generated, gold-answer-conditioned reasoning traces, specialized pretraining, task-specific SFT, iterative inference, and RL, while comparator training and inference budgets differ substantially. The reasoner-only ablation changes several factors simultaneously, and most ablations are reported on only two of six datasets. A resource-matched static or learned-selection baseline is needed.

Evidence: Test sets contain only about 200 examples each. Although the paper claims eight independent runs per dataset, it reports only point estimates, with no standard deviations, confidence intervals, paired tests, or seed-level results. This is particularly problematic for improvements of roughly 0.3–3 percentage points on several datasets.

Presentation and internal consistency: The stated 6.46-point gain is the difference between ARTIST's aggregate average and the single baseline with the best aggregate average, not the average gain over the strongest baseline on each dataset as the text says; the latter is about 3.8 points for Table 1 accuracy. TRQA accuracy also differs between Tables 1 and 2 (83.06 versus 83.34). Algorithm 1 says controller advantages are calculated from reliability means rather than the full controller rewards defined in the method. Figure 4's apple example lists three segments, including [40,100] and [200,320], while its trace discusses only [0,199] and [200,300]. These discrepancies reduce confidence in the results.

Reproducibility: Essential details are missing, including the precise five-layer encoder and patching scheme, signal normalization and preprocessing, segment representation, maximum number of interaction rounds, inference stopping/budget rules, reward weights, full optimization configuration, number and composition of SFT traces, and how GPT-5 outputs were post-processed. No code, model, or generated-data release commitment is stated.

Significance: The experiments are restricted to univariate classification or multiple-choice tasks, many with synthetic or highly constrained questions. They do not substantiate the broader motivating claims about open-ended clinical or financial reasoning, explanation, or causal diagnosis. The method is also substantially weaker than TimeMaster+RL on Sleep-QA.

Limitations and ethics: The limitations section omits major issues such as the controller's full-series access, computational cost of 36 nested reasoner samples per example, dependence on gold-answer-conditioned synthetic rationales, possible unfaithfulness of generated reasoning traces, and weak evidence for segment grounding. The generic impact statement is inadequate given evaluation on ECG and EEG tasks; medical deployment risks, calibration, failure modes, and the non-diagnostic nature of the results should be discussed. Overall, the idea has merit, but unsupported central efficiency and grounding claims, confounded evaluation, internal inconsistencies, and insufficient reproducibility currently prevent acceptance.

strengths: Originality and significance: Interleaving question-conditioned temporal segment selection with reasoning is a useful and relatively underexplored direction for time-series QA. The controller–reasoner decomposition offers an intuitive way to separate evidence acquisition from answer generation.

Soundness: The role-specific objectives are sensible: repeated reasoner rollouts provide a more stable controller reward, trajectory-level credit supports multi-step selection, and variance-guided sampling targets informative reasoner groups.

Evaluation breadth: Experiments cover six benchmarks across biomedical, environmental, financial, and general domains, with comparisons to text, time-series-encoder, and vision-language systems. The reported results are often strong, particularly on ETI, RCW, TSQA, and TRQA.

The ablations provide useful preliminary evidence for joint optimization, reliability rewards, trajectory-level controller updates, and variance-guided sampling. Qualitative examples also make the intended interaction protocol easy to understand.

Presentation is generally clear, with an explicit mathematical formulation, algorithm, dataset statistics, prompts, and several training hyperparameters. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges iterative inference cost and the restriction to univariate, regularly sampled series.
weaknesses: The central selective-information claim is not established as stated. Equation 3 and the controller prompt give the controller the full time-series embedding at every interaction round. Thus ARTIST does not avoid encoding or processing the full series; the reported 30–70% utilization measures only segments subsequently exposed to the reasoner. Repeated controller access may even increase total computation, yet latency, FLOPs, tokens, and memory are not reported.

The causal interpretation of the usage analysis is unsupported. Figure 3 bins examples by the model's chosen coverage and observes lower accuracy at high coverage, but difficult questions can simultaneously cause more retrieval and more errors. This does not show that using less data improves accuracy.

The main ablation does not cleanly isolate adaptive selection. “Reasoner Only” changes the information interface and apparently the training regime, while no compute-matched random, fixed-window, learned one-shot, oracle, or nonadaptive multi-segment baseline is included. The ablations are also limited to two of the six datasets.

Several numerical inconsistencies reduce confidence in the results. In Table 1, ARTIST's ECG-QA gain over OpenTSLM is 0.31 points (69.81 versus 69.50), not the reported 3.14. The stated 6.46-point average is the difference between ARTIST and the single baseline row with the strongest overall average, not the average gain over the strongest baseline on each dataset as claimed. TRQA is 83.06 in Table 1 but 83.34 in Table 2.

The paper says results are averaged over eight independent runs but provides no standard deviations, confidence intervals, or significance tests. With test sets of only about 200 examples and some gains below three points, it is unclear which improvements are statistically reliable.

Baseline comparability is insufficiently documented. ARTIST is trained separately on thousands of labeled examples per benchmark, while some comparators are zero-shot and others are fine-tuned; the manuscript does not fully specify whether fine-tuned baselines use identical splits, preprocessing, statistics, budgets, or model-selection procedures. The extremely poor GPT-5 and Qwen results further warrant prompt and parsing sensitivity checks.

Reproducibility remains inadequate despite the useful appendix. Reward weights, maximum interaction rounds, segment-length constraints at RL/inference time, patch size, MLP dimensions, preprocessing, token limits, seeds, baseline configurations, and exact dataset restrictions are missing. Algorithm 1 also says controller advantages are calculated from reliability means rather than the full controller rewards defined in Equation 10, and behavior when every variance is zero is unspecified. No code or artifact availability statement is given.

SFT traces are generated by GPT-5 using the gold answer and full rendered signal, then post-processed by an unspecified procedure. This can produce label-conditioned rationalizations rather than independently grounded segment supervision. The paper should disclose filtering criteria, retention rates, human verification, cost, and controls against benchmark or split leakage, especially for the modified ETI data.

The qualitative evidence is not fully consistent: the left example's displayed segment list does not match the intervals discussed in its trace, while the right example first retrieves the entire series and then an overlapping local segment. These examples weaken the claimed verifiable evidence trail and efficiency narrative.

The societal-impact discussion is boilerplate despite evaluations on ECG and EEG and motivating clinical use. It should discuss the risks of presenting benchmark pattern recognition as clinical reasoning, possible hallucinated explanations, privacy and licensing of medical datasets, and the need to prevent diagnostic deployment without validation. The limitations discussion also omits these issues and the controller's full-series access.

strengths: Originality/significance: Framing time-series question answering as iterative segment selection is useful and relatively underexplored. The controller–reasoner decomposition is intuitive and could support inspectable evidence acquisition.
Soundness: The paper evaluates six benchmarks across several domains and includes relevant ablations of the controller, reliability reward, trajectory-level objective, and variance-guided sampling.
The appendices provide dataset sizes, prompts, training costs, core optimization equations, and comparisons with dynamic visual search and time-series explainability methods.

Presentation: The paper is generally well organized, and the qualitative examples make the intended interaction protocol easy to understand. The limitations section appropriately acknowledges iterative inference cost and restriction to univariate, regularly sampled signals.
weaknesses: The central active-acquisition and efficiency interpretation is not supported by the actual architecture. Equations (3)–(4) and the controller prompt show that the controller receives the full time-series embedding at every round. ARTIST therefore does consume and encode the entire series; it only restricts what is subsequently passed to the reasoner. Claims that it avoids full-series consumption, that cost is dominated by selected segments, and that it actively acquires previously unseen information need substantial qualification and direct compute accounting for the full encoder/controller path.

The headline 6.46-point improvement is misleading. It is the difference between ARTIST's average and the best single baseline's average, not the average improvement over the strongest comparator on each dataset as the text and Table 1 footnote suggest. Using the strongest Table 1 baseline per dataset gives a much smaller gain of roughly 3.8 points. The ECG-QA improvement entry also appears inconsistent: 69.81 versus 69.50 is 0.31 points, not the reported 3.14.

The evidence does not isolate the causal value of adaptive selection. Figure 3 is observational and strongly confounded by question difficulty: difficult examples may cause both greater coverage and lower accuracy. The reasoner-only ablation simultaneously changes evidence selection, interaction, and training distribution and is reported on only two datasets. Comparisons against random, fixed, learned one-shot, oracle, and equal-segment-budget selection policies are missing.

Statistical reporting is inadequate. Test sets contain only about 200 examples, yet no standard deviations, confidence intervals, hypothesis tests, or per-run results are reported. The phrase '8 independent runs' is ambiguous as to whether these are independent training seeds or repeated stochastic inference from one checkpoint. Several claimed gains are small enough that uncertainty is decisive.

Evaluation fairness is insufficiently documented. ARTIST receives additional large-scale time-series/language pretraining, GPT-5-generated traces conditioned on the gold answer, and full-parameter RL, while baseline training budgets and pretraining exposure are not controlled. The comparison to PixelReasoner changes its backbone while claiming to keep the remaining pipeline unchanged, but provides too little adaptation detail to establish a faithful baseline.

The long-sequence experiment is weak evidence for scalability: it appends tiled, noisy copies while leaving all relevant information in the original first 4,000 positions, creating an exploitable positional prior. It does not test shifted evidence, multiple distractor locations, genuinely longer natural signals, or encoder cost scaling, despite the controller processing the full embedding.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important details are absent or unclear, including the patch encoder and tokenizer specification, patch size, maximum interaction rounds, segment constraints at inference, reward weights, precise baseline configurations, dataset conversion and split procedures, ETI augmentation details, and random seeds. The displayed website/code fields are empty. Algorithm 1 also says controller advantages are calculated from mean correctness rather than the full controller reward defined in the preceding method.

Some results undermine the broad performance narrative without adequate discussion. ARTIST is far below TimeMaster+RL on Sleep-QA (36.63 versus 72.55 accuracy), and RL materially reduces F1 on RCW and ECG-QA despite improving accuracy, suggesting class-imbalance or decision-threshold issues. The modality appendix only compares SFT variants and therefore does not resolve the reported RL gap.

Presentation has several correctness problems: Figure 4's displayed segment list does not match its accompanying reasoning trace, one example first selects the complete series despite being used to illustrate selective acquisition, and the policy-objective equations omit important conditioning variables such as the time series, interaction history, and selected segments.

Ethics and limitations are treated too superficially for experiments involving clinical ECG and EEG tasks. The generic impact statement does not discuss data governance, failure modes, subgroup performance, or the danger of interpreting benchmark multiple-choice accuracy as clinically meaningful reasoning. These concerns are not necessarily prohibitive, but they should be explicitly scoped. Overall, the idea is promising, but unsupported central efficiency claims, inconsistent headline reporting, and insufficiently controlled evidence prevent acceptance in its current form.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: query-dependent evidence acquisition can be valuable when long time series contain only a few relevant intervals.
The controller–reasoner decomposition is intuitive, and assigning trajectory-level rewards to selection while separately optimizing answer generation is a reasonable methodological direction.

The evaluation spans six datasets and several domains, and the authors include ablations, inference-cost measurements, a long-sequence experiment, qualitative examples, and comparisons with visual-search and explainability methods.
The manuscript is generally readable and visually polished. The main architecture, interaction protocol, and high-level training procedure are explained clearly.
The limitations section appropriately acknowledges additional inference cost and the current restriction to univariate, regularly sampled signals.
weaknesses: The central characterization of ARTIST as actively acquiring only selected information is misleading. Equations (3)–(4) and the controller prompt explicitly give the controller the full time series or its full embedding at every interaction. Thus, the system has already processed global information before selecting segments; selection limits only what the reasoner sees. This directly undermines claims that computation is dominated by selected segments, that the approach avoids full-series encoding, and that selective data use itself explains the gains.

The experiments do not isolate the benefit of adaptive selection from substantially greater training and inference computation. ARTIST uses repeated controller and reasoner calls plus full-parameter RL, whereas the strongest baselines are largely single-pass systems. The key 'Reasoner Only' ablation is not compute- or call-matched, and there are no random-segment, fixed learned-selector, full-series multi-turn, or oracle-segment controls. Consequently, the reported accuracy differences do not establish the paper's principal causal claim.

Several numerical summaries are inconsistent or potentially misleading. The stated 6.46-point average improvement is the difference between ARTIST and the single baseline with the best overall average, while the per-dataset 'Improvement' row is described as using the strongest baseline for each dataset and contains values that do not follow from the displayed table (for example, ECG-QA accuracy). Strong VLM results are also omitted from that headline comparison. RL materially lowers RCW F1 relative to SFT, and ARTIST remains far below TimeMaster+RL on Sleep-QA, weakening the uniformly positive account of RL.

Evidence is statistically inadequate. Test sets contain only about 200 examples, yet the paper reports no confidence intervals, seed-level standard deviations, paired tests, or significance analysis. Averaging eight stochastic inference runs over the same examples does not provide eight independent test sets. This is especially problematic for small claimed gains such as 0.31 accuracy points over OpenTSLM on ECG-QA.

The method is internally ambiguous. On an ACCEPT action, the previous reasoner answer is returned and no new reasoner step occurs, but the trajectory definition requires reasoner outputs at every round, including the terminal round. Later objectives optimize the 'final-round' reasoner output, leaving an off-by-one inconsistency. The KL term's placement in Eq. (19), behavior when all variance-guided sampling weights are zero, maximum interaction length, segment constraints, and important reward weights are also unclear or missing.

The scalability experiment does not support the stated conclusion. Appending noisy tiled copies of the original series does not obviously create uninformative data because it duplicates the original signal structure. Moreover, the claim that tripling sequence length barely affects cost conflicts with the controller being given a full-series embedding, unless an undisclosed fixed-cost compression is used.

The modality analysis changes both the backbone and input representation, so it cannot show that modality is the primary cause of the Sleep-QA gap. Its favorable comparison uses an SFT-only TimeMaster result while the main table reports a stronger TimeMaster+RL result.

Originality is moderate rather than high: the main idea transfers iterative region selection and hierarchical role-specific optimization from dynamic visual search to time series. Calling the procedure 'self-play' overstates the distinction, since both roles are optimized cooperatively using gold-answer correctness on a fixed labeled dataset.

Reproducibility is insufficient. The advertised code/website entry is blank, and essential details are missing, including the exact patch encoder and preprocessing, pretraining recipe, reward coefficients, stopping policy, tool implementation, split construction for the augmented ETI data, and complete per-dataset training information. The incomplete TRQA citation further hampers verification.

The impact statement is boilerplate. Given the clinical ECG and sleep applications invoked by the paper, it should discuss risks from incorrect or selectively grounded answers, appropriate non-clinical-use boundaries, data provenance or licensing, and privacy considerations. These omissions are not the main reason for rejection but should be corrected.

strengths: Soundness: The empirical study is broad and generally convincing: six benchmarks span clinical, environmental, financial, and general domains, with comparisons against text LLMs, time-series encoders, vision-language systems, and an adapted dynamic-search method. ARTIST raises average accuracy from 63.61% after SFT to 69.26% after RL in Table 1.

Soundness: The ablations support several design choices. On ECG-QA and RCW, removing adaptive selection, reliability rewards, trajectory-level credit assignment, or joint controller-reasoner optimization causes substantial degradation. The inference-cost, long-sequence, modality, and region-localization appendices add useful evidence beyond headline accuracy.

Originality: Separating evidence acquisition from answer generation and assigning trajectory-level and final-round objectives to the two roles is a novel and well-motivated adaptation of hierarchical/self-play training to time-series question answering.

Significance: Question-adaptive temporal localization is practically useful for long, heterogeneous signals. The reported gains are meaningful, particularly on ETI, RCW, TSQA, and TRQA, and the approach offers an interpretable list of inspected intervals.

Presentation and reproducibility: The paper is well organized, provides equations, pseudocode, prompts, dataset sizes, training hyperparameters, compute costs, and eight-run evaluation. Figures and tables are legible and the limitations section candidly acknowledges iterative inference cost and restriction to univariate, regularly sampled series. weaknesses: Soundness: The central framing overstates information acquisition. The controller prompt explicitly gives the controller the full time-series embedding at every decision, so ARTIST is better characterized as coarse-to-fine routing of information to the reasoner than as a model that avoids consuming a full-series representation. This also weakens the claim that selective data use itself causes the gains.

Soundness: The evidence does not establish that the selected segments faithfully ground the answer. Rewards depend on answer correctness and output format, not segment relevance; a controller that infers the answer from the full embedding could select plausible-looking segments afterward. The synthetic localization appendix helps, but an intervention such as masking selected regions, testing sufficiency/comprehensiveness, or comparing against random, oracle, and matched-budget fixed segments is needed.

Evaluation: The main ablation table covers only two of six datasets and reports no uncertainty or significance despite small test sets of roughly 200 examples. Eight stochastic runs are averaged, but variances are absent. Figure 3 is correlational and cannot support the conclusion that lower coverage improves accuracy because difficult questions may simply induce greater coverage.

Evaluation/presentation: The advertised 6.46-point gain is calculated against the Table 1 comparator set and does not reflect all reported baselines. In Table 2, TimeMaster+RL substantially outperforms ARTIST on Sleep-QA (72.55% versus 36.63%). The abstract should qualify the comparator set and discuss this major failure more prominently; the SFT-only VLM variant does not demonstrate that the full RL method resolves it.

Technical clarity and reproducibility: Important implementation details remain underspecified, including time-series patch size/stride, MLP dimensions, embedding/token interface, maximum interaction rounds, segment-length constraints at RL and test time, reward weights, optimization schedules, decoding/evaluation rules, and exact baseline tuning. Equations 16 and 19 also omit much of the stated conditioning state, and variance-proportional sampling is undefined when every group has zero variance.

Limitations and ethics: The impact statement is generic despite evaluation on ECG and EEG tasks and motivating clinical use. The paper should explicitly caution that benchmark accuracy and natural-language rationales do not imply clinical validity, calibrated uncertainty, causal explanation, or safe deployment. It should also discuss privacy and automation-bias risks associated with medical time series.
